query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning–based transport model that incorporates ab initio calculations of temperature‐dependent electron–phonon and electron–defect (including oxygen impurity) scattering will significantly improve predictions of electrical conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr over both the low-temperature (0–200 K) regime for near‐ideal, defect‐free samples and the high-temperature (300–1200 K) regime for samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy in two states: (a) nearly ideal, defect‐free form for 0–200 K measurements, and (b) a version intentionally doped with ~1 wt.% oxygen for 300–1200 K measurements.
generation.intervention: Implementation of a data-driven, machine learning model that integrates ab initio–calculated, temperature-dependent electron–phonon and electron–impurity scattering rates with available experimental conductivity data.
generation.conditions: Two regimes: (a) 0–200 K for defect‐free (pristine) conditions and (b) 300–1200 K for oxygen-doped samples (~1 wt.% oxygen).
generation.structural_mediator: Explicit incorporation of scattering mechanisms—such as anharmonic lattice vibrations and impurity-induced (oxygen) defect scattering—that affect electron transport in the material.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures (0–200 K), the reduced phonon population minimizes electron scattering, leading to higher conductivity; at high temperatures (300–1200 K), increased phonon activity and the introduction of oxygen impurities enhance scattering, reducing conductivity. The ML model uses ab initio scattering rates as inputs and is calibrated against experimental benchmarks to capture these effects quantitatively.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML model will yield conductivity predictions that closely match experimental values across the two temperature regimes, reducing prediction errors compared to conventional analytical models that assume perfect crystals. In particular, the model is expected to capture the enhanced scattering in the oxygen-doped high-temperature samples, resulting in a lower predicted conductivity relative to the ideal state.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical predictions which assume perfect, defect‐free crystals and thus do not account for temperature-induced scattering or oxygen impurity effects, leading to significant discrepancies from measured conductivity values.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr in: (a) the low-temperature regime (0–200 K) for nearly ideal samples and (b) the high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) for specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen. Extrapolation beyond these conditions or to significantly different impurity levels may not be reliable.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the exact quantitative correction factors and scattering rate magnitudes due to limitations in available ab initio data and experimental variability in sample purity and oxygen content. Further refinement of the scattering models and additional experimental benchmarking may be required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one set with minimal impurities (nearly defect-free) and one with controlled addition of ~1 wt.% oxygen. Measure electrical conductivity across the 0–200 K regime for the pristine samples and 300–1200 K for the oxygen-doped samples. Use consistent and well-calibrated measurement techniques to obtain high‐accuracy conductivity data.
measurements: Electrical conductivity as a function of temperature for both sets of samples.
Characterization of impurity content to confirm ~1 wt.% oxygen in the doped samples.
Comparative analysis of predicted versus measured conductivity values.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model’s predictions deviate significantly (e.g., by more than 20% relative error at any benchmark temperature point) from the experimentally measured conductivity values in either regime, this would falsify the hypothesis that the model substantially improves upon conventional analytical methods.

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

frame.goal: To achieve a predictive methodology for electrical (and/or thermal) conductivity that quantitatively matches experimental measurements over both the low-temperature (0–200 K) and high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes by incorporating the effects of defects and oxygen impurities, which conventional analytical models neglect.

decision.trend: Early work on predicting properties of high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) largely relied on analytical models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals. As research progressed, computational methods (such as atomistic simulations using ab initio and machine‐learning potentials) were developed to capture finite‐temperature effects like phonon‐phonon and electron–phonon scattering, as well as the impact of disorder. However, these efforts typically focused on mechanical or oxidation properties and rarely incorporated defect types such as oxygen impurities, leaving conductivity predictions in real, imperfect samples unsolved. The trend, therefore, has been from idealized analytical predictions toward more sophisticated, albeit still limited, computational approaches that begin to consider scattering mechanisms but do not yet deliver quantitative conductivity predictions across both low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes.
decision.unsolved: The key unsolved challenge is incorporating realistic scattering mechanisms—specifically finite‐temperature phonon and electron scattering and the additional scattering due to point defects like ~1 wt.% oxygen—into a quantitative conductivity prediction model. This remains unresolved for bulk HfNbTaTiZr both in near-ideal conditions (low T) and in oxygen-doped samples (high T), where current analytical models fall short.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning–based transport model that integrates ab initio-calculated temperature-dependent electron–phonon and electron–defect (including oxygen impurity) scattering rates with experimental conductivity data as training benchmarks. This model should explicitly account for defect-induced scattering and anharmonic lattice dynamics across the two temperature regimes.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend of moving beyond oversimplified analytical models by combining first-principles physics with data-driven calibration. Such a model will leverage prior evidence (e.g., from studies on processing and impurity effects in HfNbTaTiZr as in PMC11077685) to improve prediction accuracy. It also systematically addresses the dual regime requirements and provides concrete, testable benchmarks (e.g., a held-out conductivity value at a specific temperature) that, if not met, would falsify the hypothesis.
